notes.subject: CHEMISTRY
notes.title: Periodic Table of Elements
notes.summary: The periodic table organizes elements by atomic number. Periods are rows; groups are columns. Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionization energy and electronegativity generally increase across a period.
key_ideas: Elements ordered by increasing atomic number.
Group number relates to valence electrons for main-group elements.
Metals left, non-metals right, metalloids on the stair.
Noble gases have full outer shells and are very unreactive.

sections.heading: Organization of the periodic table
sections.explanation: The modern table uses atomic number. A period is a horizontal row. A group is a vertical column. Same group often means similar chemical behaviour because of the same number of valence electrons.

sections.heading: Metals, non-metals and metalloids
sections.explanation: Metals are typically shiny and conductive and form positive ions. Non-metals are on the right. Metalloids (e.g. Si, Ge) have intermediate properties.

sections.heading: Periodic trends
sections.explanation: Across a period radius tends to decrease. Down a group radius increases. First ionization energy generally rises across a period and falls down a group.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.explanation: Sodium (Group 1) forms Na⁺. Chlorine (Group 17) forms Cl⁻. Together they form ionic NaCl.

exercises.answer: Full outer shells — they rarely gain, lose or share electrons.

exercises.prompt: How does atomic radius change from Li to F?

notes.subject: CHEMISTRY
notes.title: Chemical Bonds and Forces
notes.summary: Ionic bonds: electron transfer. Covalent bonds: electron sharing. Intermolecular forces (including hydrogen bonding) affect boiling points and solubility.
key_ideas: Ionic compounds form lattices of ions.
Covalent molecules may be polar or non-polar.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling points.

sections.heading: Ionic bonding
sections.explanation: Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain. Electrostatic attraction holds the lattice. Example: NaCl.

sections.heading: Covalent bonding
sections.explanation: Non-metals share pairs. Single, double, triple bonds share one, two, three pairs. H₂, O₂, N₂.

sections.heading: Polarity
sections.explanation: Unequal electronegativity → polar bond. Shape matters: CO₂ non-polar overall; H₂O polar.

sections.heading: Intermolecular forces
sections.explanation: Dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonds (H with N/O/F). H-bonding explains water’s high boiling point.

exercises.answer: N donates a lone pair to H⁺.
exercises.explanation: Both electrons in that bond come from nitrogen.

notes.subject: CHEMISTRY
notes.title: Solutions and their Properties
notes.summary: Homogeneous mixtures of solute and solvent. Concentration: molarity, molality, percent by mass. Solubility depends on temperature and pressure (gases).

sections.heading: Types of solutions
sections.explanation: Unsaturated, saturated, supersaturated describe how much solute is dissolved relative to equilibrium.

sections.heading: Concentration
sections.explanation: M = n/V. Molality = n/kg solvent. Percent by mass = (mass solute/mass solution)×100%.

sections.heading: Dilution
sections.explanation: Moles stay constant: C₁V₁=C₂V₂. Example: 50 mL of 12 M → 1 M needs 600 mL.

sections.heading: Solubility factors
sections.explanation: Most solid solubility rises with temperature. Gas solubility falls with temperature and rises with pressure.

exercises.prompt: Why does a warm fizzy drink go flat faster?
exercises.answer: Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises.

notes.subject: CHEMISTRY
notes.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
notes.summary: Acids produce H⁺ in water; bases produce OH⁻. pH=−log[H⁺]. Neutralization forms salt + water.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.explanation: Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry views. HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.

sections.heading: pH scale
sections.explanation: pH=−log[H⁺]. 0.01 M HCl → pH=2. Pure water → pH=7.

sections.heading: Neutralization
sections.explanation: HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H₂O. Titration finds unknown concentration.

sections.heading: Strength vs concentration
sections.explanation: Strength = extent of ionization. Concentration = amount per litre.

exercises.explanation: Two H⁺ neutralized by two OH⁻.

notes.subject: CHEMISTRY
notes.title: Chemical Reactions and Stoichiometry
notes.summary: Balanced equations conserve atoms. The mole links mass and particles. Limiting reactant controls product amount.

sections.heading: Balancing
sections.explanation: Same number of each atom on both sides. 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O.

sections.heading: Mole calculations
sections.explanation: n=m/M. Use coefficients as mole ratios. Identify limiting reactant.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.explanation: Theoretical vs actual yield; percent yield compares them.

sections.heading: Reaction types
sections.explanation: Combination, decomposition, single and double displacement.

exercises.prompt: Moles CO₂ from 2 mol CH₄ complete combustion?
